text:
Going up toward San Félix, where the river shows two teeth,

where the river shows, tightly clenched,

the two fists of Piar squeezing the Deed,

going up toward San Félix, we saw the rainbow

that made the Indian bow on its string of waters.

And then I remembered, friends,

that lesson in History we read in childhood,

the first lesson in History,

in which our legend inaugurates the soul:

Remember the first lesson:

it tells us that Columbus discovered us on his third voyage

and speaks of those currents that stopped Columbus.


A simple History class, clear as a morning,

simple as the day of the first sweetheart,

the dream of first dawns,

a simple History class, like a Sunday,

with eight o'clock Mass and starched clothes,

a History class that tells us of the day

when the caravels from Spain were coming,

while, indifferent to everything that might come from the sea,

Sorocaima searched the mountains for flowers for his beloved.

Through the stormy strait,

the three caravels advance,

another sail is raised in the foam

that fans the stones of the coast of Paria,

the three caravels come,

but on the Indians' side the twenty mouths await them.


And as they head toward the free Ocean,

a shadow rises;

its legs spread across the Delta,

clinging to the soil that keeps its treasures,

the Orinoco of its wet thighs,

with gold in its feet and the Sun on its back

and its head among the heavens,

in one hand it holds a bow and shoots twenty arrows,

and the three ships struggle to advance in vain

because at the Delta they are repelled by

the old autonomous Indian,

who was born in Parima and grew up in Guayana,

and draws the indigenous bow—yes, draws the rainbow bow—

and shoots twenty arrows as twenty herons fly…

translation.title: Indigenous Evocation
translation.editorial_note: The translation retains the historical names and the final transformation of the Indigenous bow into a rainbow bow.
